exercises.prompt: Implement mergeObjects(a, b) so it returns a new object holding all the properties of a and b, without modifying either input. When both objects have the same key, b's value wins. mergeObjects({a: 1}, {a: 2}) is {a: 2}. Two empty objects return an empty object.
hints: Spreading an object into a new object literal copies its properties out: { ...a } is a shallow copy of a.
Spread both, in order — the later spread overwrites keys the earlier one set, which is exactly why b should come second.
return { ...a, ...b } — building a fresh literal means the caller's base object is never touched, as the last test checks.

exercises.prompt: Implement headAndRest(arr) so it returns a two-element array [first, rest]: first is arr's first element, and rest is a new array of all the remaining elements. headAndRest([1, 2, 3]) is [1, [2, 3]]. For a single-element array the rest is []. For an empty array, first is undefined and rest is [].
hints: Array destructuring can name the first element and gather everything after it in one line.
A rest element in the pattern collects the leftovers into a real array: const [first, ...rest] = arr.
const [first, ...rest] = arr; return [first, rest] — on an empty array first is undefined and rest is [] with no extra handling.

exercises.prompt: Implement withDefaults(opts) so it returns a complete settings object, filling in any field that opts omits from these defaults: {color: 'black', size: 'M', qty: 1}. Any field opts provides overrides the default — including a provided 0 or '' — and withDefaults({}) returns exactly the defaults. Do not modify opts.
hints: Lay the defaults down first, then spread opts on top so anything the caller supplied replaces the matching default.
Order is everything: the defaults must appear before ...opts, or the defaults would overwrite the caller's values.
return { color: 'black', size: 'M', qty: 1, ...opts } — because ...opts overrides by key, a provided qty of 0 correctly replaces the default 1, where qty || 1 would not.

exercises.prompt: Implement greet(opts), where opts is an object with a name and an optional greeting, so it returns the string `${greeting}, ${name}`. When greeting is missing, default it to 'Hello'. greet({name: 'Sam'}) is 'Hello, Sam' and greet({name: 'Sam', greeting: 'Hi'}) is 'Hi, Sam'. Use object destructuring with a default value.
hints: Object destructuring can name the fields you want and supply a fallback for a missing one in the same pattern.
A default in the pattern kicks in only when the property is absent: const { name, greeting = 'Hello' } = opts.
const { name, greeting = 'Hello' } = opts; return `${greeting}, ${name}` — the default fills greeting whenever opts leaves it out.

exercises.prompt: Implement concatAll(...arrays) so it accepts any number of array arguments and returns a single new array with all their elements in order. concatAll([1, 2], [3], [4, 5]) is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Called with no arguments it returns []. Use a rest parameter to gather the arrays.
hints: A rest parameter ...arrays gathers however many arguments were passed into one array of arrays.
concat joins arrays end to end, and spreading your gathered arrays feeds them all in as separate arguments: [].concat(...arrays).
return [].concat(...arrays) — with no arguments, arrays is [] and the spread contributes nothing, so you get [].
